module_metadata.title: MODULE 6: DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES — UNDERSTANDING CHILD DEVELOPMENT FROM 0–5
module_metadata.certificate: Baby First Health Early Childhood Development Certificate
module_metadata.target_learners: Parents, caregivers, childcare workers, teachers, health practitioners, and anyone working with children aged 0–5.

sections.title: Welcome to the Module
content: Two children are both three years old. One speaks constantly and loves talking to adults. The other is quieter but enjoys building blocks and communicates well through gestures and short sentences.
Does developing differently automatically mean one child has a problem?
No. Children develop at different rates and in different ways. Variation is normal.[1][2][3]

This module will help you understand what developmental milestones are, how they can be used to follow a child's development, what children generally learn and do from birth to age five, and how to recognize when a child may benefit from further developmental assessment. The goal is not to make parents memorize long lists of milestones. The goal is to help you observe, understand, support, and appropriately respond to a child's development.[2][3][4][1]

sections.title: What Are Developmental Milestones?
content: Developmental milestones are skills or behaviors that most children (about 75% or more) can do by a certain age.[5][1][2]
why_milestones_are_used: Milestones describe skills children commonly develop.[1][2]
Milestones help adults notice development and identify possible concerns early.[2][5][1]
Milestones encourage ongoing conversations between families and professionals about a child's development.[5][2]
important_notes: Children do not all develop at exactly the same speed.[3][1][2]
Milestones are guides for observation, not a competition.[2][3]
Milestone checklists are not diagnostic tools.[6][1][2]

sections.title: The Four Main Developmental Areas
content: Children's development is often described in four main areas. These areas are connected and often develop together.[4][1][3]

areas.name: Social and Emotional
areas.description: How children learn to relate to other people and understand their own feelings.

areas.name: Language and Communication
areas.description: How children understand and use language to communicate.

areas.name: Cognitive
areas.description: How children learn, think, remember, and solve problems.
examples: Problem-solving (figuring out how a toy works)

areas.name: Physical and Motor
areas.description: How children use their bodies, including large movements and small hand movements.
examples: Gross motor skills (large movements): Sitting, crawling, walking, running, jumping, climbing[6][1]
Fine motor skills (small hand movements): Reaching, grasping, picking up small objects, scribbling, using a spoon, buttoning[1][6]

sections.important_note: Important: These areas are connected. For example, language, movement, thinking, and social interaction often develop together. A child who is learning to walk (physical) may also be learning to point and communicate wants (language and social).[4][3][1]

sections.title: Developmental Milestones From Birth to Age 5
content: This section provides a clear, learner-friendly overview of broad developmental milestones. This is not an overwhelming encyclopedia of hundreds of milestones. The exact timing of these skills varies between children.[3][2][6][1]

sections.title: Milestones Are Not a Competition
why_comparison_is_unhelpful: Development is influenced by many factors: genetics, temperament, opportunities for practice, environment, language exposure, health, nutrition, sleep, and individual differences.[4][3][2][1]
A child being ahead in one area and slower in another does not automatically indicate a problem.[3][2][1]
Social media often shows unrealistic or selective images of child development.[2][1]

sections.title: Developmental Variation
content: Normal variation means that children develop at different rates and in different ways. This is expected and healthy.[1][2][3]
influencing_factors: Different rates of development – Some children develop skills earlier; others develop later.[2][1]
Different strengths – A child may be advanced in one area (e.g., physical) and developing more typically in another (e.g., language).[3][1]
Temperament – Some children are naturally more outgoing; others are more cautious or quiet.[2][3]
Opportunities for practice – Children who have more opportunities to practice certain skills may develop those skills earlier.[4][1]
Environment – Safe, stimulating environments support development.[8][4][1]
Language exposure – Children who hear more conversation, reading, and singing typically have more language-learning opportunities.[4][1]
Health – Illness, chronic conditions, or disabilities can affect development.[4][1]
Nutrition – Good nutrition supports brain development and overall growth.[8][4]
Sleep – Adequate sleep is important for brain development and learning.[1][4]
Individual differences – Every child is unique.[3][1][2]
sections.important_note: Important: A child being ahead in one area and slower in another does not automatically indicate a problem. Development is uneven and varies across domains.[1][2][3]

sections.title: Milestones and Multilingual Children
content: Children exposed to multiple languages should be understood in the context of their language environment. Multilingualism itself should not automatically be treated as a developmental delay.[2][3][1]
key_points: Multiple languages at home – Children may hear two or more languages from different family members.[1][2]
Different amounts of exposure to each language – A child may hear one language more at home and another at school or in the community.[2][1]
Vocabulary distributed across languages – A child may know some words in one language and other words in another language. Total vocabulary across all languages should be considered.[3][1][2]
Code-switching – Mixing words or phrases from two or more languages in one conversation or sentence is normal in bilingual and multilingual development.[1][2]
Language mixing – Using words from different languages together is a natural part of learning multiple languages.[2][1]
when_discussing_concerns: Assessment should consider the child's overall communication abilities across the languages they use, not just one language. A child may appear to have limited vocabulary in one language but have a typical total vocabulary when all languages are considered.[3][1][2]

sections.title: How Adults Can Observe Development
content: Observation can happen naturally during everyday activities. Observation should not turn everyday life into a constant test.[3][1][2]
what_to_observe: Whether skills are progressing over time[2][3][1]
how_to_observe: Watch the child during natural activities.
Notice what the child does independently.
Notice what the child does with support.
Notice changes over weeks and months, not just day-to-day.
Consider the child's overall development across all areas (social, emotional, language, cognitive, physical).[3][1][2]
sections.important_note: Important: Observation should be relaxed and natural, not stressful or test-like. The goal is to understand the child, not to judge or compare.[1][2][3]

sections.title: Developmental Screening vs Diagnosis
content: It is important to understand the difference between monitoring, screening, and diagnosis.[5][2][3][1]
developmental_monitoring: Regularly observing and discussing how a child is developing.
Happens continuously through everyday interactions and well-child visits.
Involves noticing milestones, asking about caregiver concerns, and discussing development with health professionals.[5][2][3][1]
developmental_screening: A structured process used by qualified professionals to identify children who may need further evaluation.
Uses validated screening tools (e.g., Ages and Stages Questionnaire, Parents' Evaluation of Developmental Status).
Recommended at specific ages (e.g., 9, 18, and 30 months) by the American Academy of Pediatrics.[5][2][3][1]
Screening is not a diagnosis. It identifies children who may need more detailed assessment.[2][1][6]
developmental_evaluation_assessment: A more detailed professional assessment when a concern has been identified.
Conducted by specialists (e.g., developmental pediatricians, psychologists, speech-language therapists).
Helps determine if a child has a developmental delay or disability and what support may be needed.[3][1][2]
important_notes: A milestone checklist is not a diagnosis.[1][2][6]
Milestone checklists are tools to support developmental surveillance, not to diagnose conditions.[5][2][1]
If concerns arise during monitoring or screening, further evaluation may be recommended.[5][2][3][1]

sections.title: When Should Parents Be Concerned?
content: This section explains situations that deserve discussion with a qualified professional (such as a pediatrician, early childhood specialist, or developmental therapist). This information is not diagnostic.[2][3][1]
situations_for_professional_discussion: The child is consistently missing important expected skills – The child does not show skills that most children of their age can do.[3][1][2]
Development appears significantly behind in one or more areas – The child's development is notably delayed compared to typical expectations.[1][2][3]
There is little or no progress over time – The child does not seem to be gaining new skills over weeks or months.[2][3][1]
The child has difficulty functioning in everyday activities – The child's development significantly interferes with daily life at home, in childcare, or in the community.[3][1][2]
Multiple developmental areas are affected – Delays are present in several areas (e.g., language, social, physical).[1][2][3]
Parents or caregivers have persistent concerns – Caregivers feel worried about the child's development over time. Parental concern is an important indicator.[5][2][3][1]
A child loses a skill they previously had – The child had certain skills and then lost them (regression).[2][3][1][6]
important_notes: Loss of previously acquired skills should always be discussed promptly with an appropriate healthcare or developmental professional. Regression can be a sign of a serious concern and should not be ignored.[3][1][2][6]
One missed milestone does not automatically mean something is wrong. Concerns should be persistent and significant.[1][2][3]
Do not diagnose conditions. Only qualified professionals can diagnose developmental delays or disabilities.[2][3][1]
Do not create unnecessary fear. Many children develop more slowly in some areas and catch up with time and support.[3][1][2]

sections.title: What Parents Should Do If They Have Concerns
content: If you have concerns about a child's development, follow these practical steps:[1][2][3][6]
practical_steps: Observe the concern – Notice what the child can and cannot do. Pay attention to patterns over time, not just one day.[2][1]
Write down specific examples – Note specific behaviors or skills that concern you. Include dates and contexts.[1][2]
Avoid comparing the child with other children – Every child develops at their own pace. Comparison can create unnecessary worry.[3][2][1]

Discuss concerns with the child's healthcare provider or qualified developmental professional – Share your observations and concerns with a pediatrician, nurse, or early childhood specialist.[2][3][1][6]
Ask whether developmental screening is appropriate – Request a developmental screening if you have concerns. Screening can help identify whether further evaluation is needed.[5][3][1][2]
Follow recommended assessments or referrals – If screening suggests further evaluation, follow through with referrals to specialists or early intervention services.[3][1][2]
Continue supporting the child's development at home – Provide rich, nurturing experiences: talking, reading, playing, singing, and responsive caregiving.[8][4][1][2]
important_notes: Early support can be valuable when a genuine developmental concern exists. Early intervention services can help children develop skills and reach their potential.[5][1][2][3]
Do not wait if you have significant concerns. Acting early can make a real difference.[1][2][6]

case_study.title: 12. African Family Case Study
case_study.context: Chidi is 2½ years old. He lives in Enugu, Nigeria. He is physically active, loves to run and climb, and understands simple instructions at home (

). He communicates well through gestures, pointing, and short sentences (1–2 words). However, Chidi uses very few spoken words compared to other children his age that his mother knows.

Chidi's mother is worried. She mentions her concern to a relative, who says:
Chidi's mother is not sure what to do. She loves her son and wants to support him, but she wonders if she should wait or seek advice.

discussion_questions.question: 1. Is the relative's advice (
) accurate?
discussion_questions.model_answer: No. While there is variation in when children start speaking, the statement
is a generalization that is not supported by evidence. Some boys do speak later, but many boys speak on time or early. Gender alone does not determine when a child will speak. Assuming
can lead to delayed identification of genuine concerns.[2][3][1]

discussion_questions.question: 2. What developmental areas should Chidi's mother consider when thinking about his development?
discussion_questions.model_answer:
Chidi's mother should look at the whole child:
Social & emotional: Is Chidi engaging with others, smiling, showing emotions, playing?
Communication: Is Chidi understanding language? Using gestures? Making sounds? Trying to communicate?
Cognitive: Is Chidi exploring, solving simple problems, pretending?
Physical: Is Chidi moving, running, climbing, using his hands?
Chidi appears to be doing well in physical and cognitive areas and understands language. The concern is primarily about expressive language (spoken words). Looking at the whole child helps avoid focusing only on one area.[3][1][2][6]

discussion_questions.question: 3. Why is hearing an important consideration when there are concerns about speech or language?
discussion_questions.model_answer: Hearing difficulties can affect speech and language development. A child who cannot hear well may have difficulty learning to speak. If there are concerns about speech or language, hearing should be checked by a qualified professional.[1][2][3]

discussion_questions.question: 4. When might professional assessment be appropriate for Chidi?
discussion_questions.model_answer:
Professional assessment may be appropriate if:
Chidi continues to use very few words over the next few months with little progress.
Chidi has difficulty being understood by familiar adults.
Chidi shows concerns in multiple developmental areas, not just language.
Chidi's mother has persistent concerns despite reassurance.
At 2½ years, many children are using 50 or more words and combining two words together. If Chidi is significantly below this, discussing with a pediatrician or early childhood specialist would be reasonable.[2][3][1][6]

discussion_questions.question: 5. What should Chidi's mother avoid doing?
discussion_questions.model_answer:
without monitoring progress.
Comparing Chidi to other children or the relative's son.
Ignoring her own concerns because someone else said not to worry.
Creating unnecessary panic or fear.
Instead, she should observe Chidi's development over time, continue providing rich language experiences (talking, reading, singing), and discuss concerns with a healthcare provider if they persist.[3][1][2][6]

practical_activity.title: 13. Practical Activity: Milestone Observation
practical_activity.instructions: Choose a child you regularly care for and observe them during normal play or routine activities. This is an educational observation exercise, not a diagnostic test.[1][2][3]

observation_table.What I Observed: (e.g., smiles at caregiver, plays near other children)
(e.g., stacks blocks, looks for hidden toy)
(e.g., walks alone, picks up small objects)

how_to_use: Observe the child during everyday activities (playing, eating, bathing, reading).
Write down what you notice in each developmental area.
Focus on what the child can do, not only what they cannot do.
Notice what skills the child seems to be practicing or working on.
Review your observations over weeks or months to see progress.
important_notes: This is an educational observation exercise, not a diagnostic test.[2][3][1]
Do not use this to compare children or create worry.
Use this to understand the child's strengths and areas for support.
If you have significant concerns based on your observations, discuss with a healthcare provider.[3][1][2][6]

common_mistakes_adults_make.title: 14. Common Mistakes Adults Make
common_mistakes_adults_make.content: Here are common mistakes adults make when thinking about developmental milestones. This section is practical and non-judgmental; we all make mistakes, and awareness helps us improve.[1][2][3]
mistakes: Treating milestone ages as exact deadlines – Milestones are guides, not strict deadlines. Children develop at different rates.[2][3][1]
Comparing children – Comparing siblings, cousins, or classmates creates unnecessary worry and does not help the child.[3][1][2]
Using social media as a developmental standard – Social media often shows unrealistic or selective images of child development.[1][2]
Assuming boys and girls must develop in completely different ways – While there is some variation, gender alone does not determine developmental timing. Avoid stereotypes like
– Some children do catch up, but persistent concerns should be discussed with a professional. Waiting too long can delay support.[3][1][2][6]
Panicking over one missed skill – One missed milestone does not automatically mean something is wrong. Look at the overall pattern of development.[1][2][3]
Treating a checklist as a diagnosis – Milestone checklists are not diagnostic tools. Only qualified professionals can diagnose developmental delays or disabilities.[2][1][6]
Forgetting to consider hearing or health – Hearing difficulties, health problems, or chronic conditions can affect development. These should be considered when there are concerns.[3][1][2]
Ignoring loss of previously acquired skills – Regression (losing skills) should always be discussed promptly with a healthcare professional.[1][2][3][6]
Focusing only on weaknesses instead of the child's strengths – Notice what the child can do, not only what they cannot do. Celebrate progress and strengths.[2][3][1]

key_takeaways.title: 15. Key Takeaways
takeaways: Developmental milestones are skills that most children (about 75% or more) can do by a certain age. They are guides, not exact deadlines.[5][1][2]
There are four main developmental areas: social and emotional, language and communication, cognitive, and physical/motor. These areas are connected.[3][1][2][6]
Children develop at different rates. Variation is normal and expected.[1][2][3]
Milestones are guides for observation, not a competition. Avoid comparing children.[2][3][1]
Multilingual children may show different language patterns. Assessment should consider the child's overall communication across all languages they use.[3][1][2]
Developmental monitoring is ongoing observation. Developmental screening is a structured process used by professionals. Screening is not a diagnosis.[5][1][2][3]

Concerns that warrant professional discussion include: consistently missing important skills, significant delays, little or no progress over time, difficulty functioning in daily life, multiple areas affected, persistent caregiver concerns, or loss of previously acquired skills.[1][2][3][6]
Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) should always be discussed promptly with a healthcare or developmental professional.[2][3][1][6]
If you have concerns, observe, write down specific examples, avoid comparison, and discuss with a healthcare provider. Ask about developmental screening if appropriate.[3][1][2][6]
Early support can be valuable when a genuine developmental concern exists. Acting early can make a real difference.[5][1][2][3]

knowledge_check.instructions: Choose the best answer for each question. Only one answer is correct.

questions.question: Question 1: What is a developmental milestone?

options.A: A skill that all children must achieve by an exact age.
options.B: A skill that most children (about 75% or more) can do by a certain age.
options.C: A diagnostic tool used to identify developmental disabilities.
options.D: A test that determines if a child is intelligent.

questions.explanation: Developmental milestones are skills or behaviors that most children (about 75% or more) can do by a certain age. They are guides for observation, not exact deadlines or diagnostic tools.[5][1][2]

questions.question: Question 2: Which of the following is an example of a fine motor skill?

options.B: Jumping off the ground with both feet.
options.C: Picking up small objects using thumb and index finger.

questions.explanation: Fine motor skills involve small hand movements, such as picking up small objects using the pincer grasp (thumb and index finger). Running, jumping, and climbing are gross motor skills (large movements).[1][6]

questions.question: Question 3: A parent is worried because their 18-month-old child is not yet speaking in sentences, but the child understands simple instructions, uses gestures, and says several single words. What is the best response?

options.A: This definitely indicates a serious developmental delay.
options.B: This is definitely normal; there is no need for any concern.
options.C: Understanding often develops before speaking. Continue observing and providing rich language experiences. Discuss with a healthcare provider if concerns persist.
options.D: The child should be speaking in sentences by 18 months, so this is a serious concern.

questions.explanation: Understanding (receptive language) often develops before speaking (expressive language). Many children understand more than they can say. Continuing to observe and provide rich language experiences is appropriate. If concerns persist, discussing with a healthcare provider is recommended.[2][3][1][6]

questions.question: Question 4: What should a parent do if they notice their child has lost a skill they previously had (e.g., the child was saying several words and then stopped)?

options.A: Wait and see if the child regains the skill on their own.
options.B: Assume this is normal variation and do nothing.
options.C: Discuss this promptly with a healthcare or developmental professional.
options.D: Compare the child to other children to see if they also lost skills.

questions.explanation: Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) should always be discussed promptly with a healthcare or developmental professional. Regression can be a sign of a serious concern and should not be ignored.[3][1][2][6]

questions.question: Question 5: A child is learning two languages at home (English and Yoruba). The child knows some words in English and other words in Yoruba. The parent is worried this means the child is delayed. What is the best response?

options.A: The child should only learn one language to avoid delay.
options.B: This is normal for multilingual children. Total vocabulary across both languages should be considered.
options.C: The child is definitely delayed and needs immediate therapy.
options.D: The child should stop speaking Yoruba and only speak English.

questions.explanation: Multilingual children often have vocabulary distributed across languages. This is normal. Assessment should consider the child's overall communication across all languages they use, not just one language. Multilingualism itself does not cause delay.[1][2][3]

questions.question: Question 6: What is the difference between developmental monitoring and developmental screening?

options.A: Monitoring is done by parents; screening is done by professionals using validated tools.
options.B: Monitoring and screening are the same thing.
options.C: Monitoring is a diagnosis; screening is just observation.
options.D: Monitoring is only for babies; screening is only for older children.

questions.explanation: Developmental monitoring is ongoing observation by parents, caregivers, and professionals during everyday interactions and well-child visits. Developmental screening is a structured process using validated tools, typically conducted by professionals at specific ages. Screening is not a diagnosis.[5][2][3][1]

questions.question: Question 7: Which of the following is a situation that warrants discussion with a qualified professional?

options.A: The child occasionally has a tantrum.
options.B: The child is quieter than their cousin.
options.C: The child has lost a skill they previously had.
options.D: The child prefers one toy over another.

questions.explanation: Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) should always be discussed promptly with a healthcare or developmental professional. Occasional tantrums, being quieter than a cousin, and toy preferences are normal variations.[2][3][1][6]

questions.question: Question 8: A parent notices their 3-year-old child is not yet drawing a circle, but the child is speaking in sentences, playing cooperatively with other children, and running and climbing well. What is the best response?

options.A: This definitely indicates a serious developmental delay.
options.B: This is definitely normal; there is no need for any concern.
options.C: Children develop at different rates. Look at the overall pattern of development. Continue observing and providing opportunities for practice. Discuss with a healthcare provider if concerns persist.
options.D: The child should be drawing a circle by 3 years, so this is a serious concern.

questions.explanation: Children develop at different rates. One missed skill does not automatically mean something is wrong. Looking at the overall pattern of development is important. If the child is doing well in other areas, continuing to observe and provide opportunities for practice is appropriate. If concerns persist, discussing with a healthcare provider is recommended.[3][1][2][6]

questions.question: Question 9: What is a common mistake adults make when thinking about developmental milestones?

options.A: Treating milestone ages as exact deadlines.
options.B: Observing the child during everyday activities.
options.C: Discussing concerns with a healthcare provider.
options.D: Noticing what the child can do.

questions.explanation: Treating milestone ages as exact deadlines is a common mistake. Milestones are guides, not strict deadlines. Children develop at different rates. Observing the child, discussing concerns with a healthcare provider, and noticing what the child can do are all positive practices.[1][2][3]

questions.question: Question 10: A parent has persistent concerns about their child's development, but a relative says,
What should the parent do?

options.B: Compare their child to the relative's child.
options.C: Observe, write down specific examples, and discuss concerns with a healthcare provider.
options.D: Assume the relative is correct and do nothing.

questions.explanation: Parental concern is an important indicator. If a parent has persistent concerns, they should observe, write down specific examples, and discuss with a healthcare provider. Ignoring concerns or comparing to other children is not helpful.[2][3][1][6]

short_glossary.definition: A skill or behavior that most children (about 75% or more) can do by a certain age. Milestones are guides, not exact deadlines.[5][1][2]
Regularly observing and discussing how a child is developing. Happens continuously through everyday interactions and well-child visits.[5][3][1][2]
A structured process used by qualified professionals to identify children who may need further evaluation. Uses validated screening tools. Screening is not a diagnosis.[5][3][1][2]
A more detailed professional evaluation when a concern has been identified. Conducted by specialists to determine if a child has a developmental delay or disability.[3][1][2]
Normal differences in how children develop. Children develop at different rates and in different ways. Variation is expected and healthy.[1][2][3]
Large body movements such as sitting, crawling, walking, running, jumping, and climbing.[1][6]
Small hand movements such as reaching, grasping, picking up small objects, scribbling, using a spoon, and buttoning.[1][6]
How children learn to relate to other people, understand their own feelings, express emotions, build relationships, and develop confidence.[2][3][1][6]
Understanding language—what a child comprehends when others speak.[3][2][1]
Using sounds, words, gestures, or sentences to communicate.[2][3][1]
A persistent pattern of behavior or development that significantly differs from what is expected for a child's age and may warrant discussion with a qualified professional.[3][2][1][6]

disclaimers: This module is educational and provides general information about developmental milestones and child development from birth to age 5 years. It does not diagnose developmental delays, disabilities, or other conditions.[2][3][1]
Milestones are general developmental guides. They are not diagnostic tools. Children develop at different rates, and variation is normal.[5][3][1][2]
Parents and caregivers should discuss persistent concerns with an appropriate qualified professional (such as a pediatrician, early childhood specialist, or developmental therapist).[3][1][2][6]

Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) should be discussed promptly with a healthcare or developmental professional. Regression can be a sign of a serious concern and should not be ignored.[1][2][3][6]
Urgent medical concerns require appropriate medical attention. If a child shows signs of serious illness, injury, or distress, seek medical help immediately.[2][3][1]
This module is not a substitute for standardized, validated developmental screening tools or professional evaluation.[1][2][6]
